title: They're not ready to meet my family.
old_caption: Hearing "not yet" about meeting your family can sting. Not yet isn't never. Get curious instead of hurt, and ask what would make it easier.

title: The Check-In Word
old_caption: Walking into a loud family gathering can be a lot. Agree on one check-in word before you go in: it means "check on me," and you step out together. Save this for your next visit.

title: The Ex Question
old_caption: When someone asks about your ex in front of your new partner, you don't owe the whole story. Keep it short, keep it kind, then bring the conversation back to now.

title: Quiet Isn't Unhappy
old_caption: If your partner goes quiet at your family's table, try not to guess what it means. Ask them in private and offer a break. Some people enjoy the room by listening.

title: The Baby Photos
old_caption: The baby photos came out. Laugh along, it's how families say they love you. One kind "okay, last one" is fine, and partners, be sweet about it. Who has the most embarrassing album?

title: Offer to Help
old_caption: Want to help at your partner's family dinner? Offer once, warmly. If they say no, believe them, then find a small job like the dishes. Help the way they like help.

title: Not in the Guest Room
old_caption: Tension during a holiday stay is normal. Skip the whisper-fight in the guest room: name it, take a walk together, and talk it through outside the house.

title: Back Them Up
old_caption: If a relative teases your partner, back them up in the moment, with a calm voice and no scene. Then check in with them later. Tag someone who always has your back.

title: Homesick at Their Table
old_caption: Your first holiday away from your own family can feel bittersweet, even at a warm table. It's okay to miss home out loud. Make a little room for both.

title: The Family Photo
old_caption: Not sure if you belong in their family photo? Just ask. "In or out?" is a kind question, and either answer is fine. Send this to someone meeting the family this year.
